hints: Only the horizontal component of the pushing force acts in the direction of the horizontal displacement: $F_x = 35\cos 20^\circ$.
Use the work formula $W = F_x \times d = (35\cos 20^\circ) \times 12$.
Evaluate the product and round to 3 significant figures: $395\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Resolve the pushing force of $35\text{ N}$ along the horizontal direction of motion:
$$F_x = 35\cos 20^\circ \approx 32.8892\text{ N}$$

Calculate the work done by the man over the displacement $d = 12\text{ m}$:
$$W = F_x \times d = (35\cos 20^\circ) \times 12 = 420\cos 20^\circ \approx 394.67\text{ J} \approx 395\text{ J}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
State the definition of work done by a constant force acting at an angle $\theta$ to the displacement:
$$W = (F\cos\theta) \times d$$
Identify the given values: the magnitude of the pushing force is $F = 35\text{ N}$, the angle with the horizontal is $\theta = 20^\circ$, and the horizontal distance moved is $d = 12\text{ m}$.

Substitute these values into the formula:
$$W = (35\cos 20^\circ) \times 12$$

Evaluate $\cos 20^\circ \approx 0.939693$ and calculate the final product:
$$W \approx 420 \times 0.939693 \approx 394.671\text{ J} = 395\text{ J} \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$

hints: Use the work-energy balance: Work done by the man = Work done against resistance + Gain in kinetic energy.
Calculate the work done against the constant $15\text{ N}$ resistance over $12\text{ m}$: $W_{\text{res}} = 15 \times 12 = 180\text{ J}$.
The gain in kinetic energy from rest ($u = 0$) to final speed $v$ is $\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(25)v^2 = 12.5v^2$.
Set up $394.67 = 180 + 12.5v^2$, subtract $180$, divide by $12.5$, and take the square root to find $v$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the work done against the constant resistance force of $15\text{ N}$ over the distance of $12\text{ m}$:
$$W_{\text{res}} = 15 \times 12 = 180\text{ J}$$

Apply the work-energy principle, equating the work done by the man to the sum of the work done against resistance and the kinetic energy gained from rest:
$$W_{\text{man}} = W_{\text{res}} + \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$
$$420\cos 20^\circ = 180 + \frac{1}{2}(25)v^2$$
$$394.671 = 180 + 12.5v^2$$

Solve for the final speed $v$ of the wheelbarrow:
$$12.5v^2 = 394.671 - 180 = 214.671$$
$$v^2 = \frac{214.671}{12.5} \approx 17.1737$$
$$v = \sqrt{17.1737} \approx 4.1441\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 4.14\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
State the work-energy principle for a body accelerated by an applied force against resistance on horizontal ground:
$$W_{\text{applied}} = W_{\text{resistance}} + \Delta E_k$$

Compute the work done against the resistive force:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = F_{\text{res}} \times d = 15 \times 12 = 180\text{ J}$$

Write the expression for the kinetic energy gained from rest ($u = 0$):
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(25)v^2 = 12.5v^2$$

Substitute the work done by the man ($W_{\text{man}} = 420\cos 20^\circ\text{ J}$) from part (i) into the work-energy equation:
$$420\cos 20^\circ = 180 + 12.5v^2$$

Divide both sides by $12.5$ to isolate $v^2$:
$$v^2 = \frac{214.671}{12.5} \approx 17.17368$$

Take the square root to calculate the speed $v$:
$$v = \sqrt{17.17368} \approx 4.14411\text{ m s}^{-1} = 4.14\text{ m s}^{-1} \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$

ai_rubric.Applying the Work\u2013Energy Principle: Finds work against resistance $180\text{ J}$, forms $394.67 = 180 + 12.5v^2$, and solves for $v = 4.14\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
